message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and to ensure they receive a safe, habitable living environment. Below is an overview of key rights you should know: | Category | Key Rights | What It Means | |----------|------------|---------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may not charge more than one month’s rent for a furnished unit or two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit.
• Landlord must return the deposit (or a written statement of deductions) within 30 days after the lease ends, unless the tenant agrees otherwise. | You can recover your full deposit if the landlord fails to comply. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, etc.).
• Landlord must repair any major defects that affect health or safety. | If the landlord neglects repairs, you may withhold rent or take legal action. | | **Rent Payment** | • Landlord cannot demand rent before the lease starts or after it ends.
• Landlord must provide a written receipt if requested. | You’re not obligated to pay rent until the lease period begins. | | **Lease Terms** | • Landlord cannot change the lease terms without your consent.
• Any changes must be in writing and signed by both parties. | You can refuse to sign a new lease if it contains unreasonable changes. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑renewal or termination, the landlord must give at least 30 days’ notice.
• For eviction, the landlord must follow the proper legal process (notice, court filing, etc.). | You have time to find a new place or contest an eviction. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must give reasonable notice (usually 24 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | Your right to privacy is protected. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected characteristics. | You can file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights if discrimination occurs. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but only if you follow the proper procedure. | This is a last resort; you must document the issue and notify the landlord first. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for damages, breach of contract, or unlawful eviction.
• You can seek a court order to compel repairs or to stop harassment. | You have recourse if the landlord violates your rights. | ### Practical Steps If You Encounter Problems 1. **Document Everything** – Keep records of all communications, receipts, photos of damage, and any notices received. 2. **Notify the Landlord in Writing** – Send a certified letter or email detailing the issue and requesting a remedy. 3. **Know the Timeline** – Most repairs must be completed within a reasonable time; if the landlord fails, you may withhold rent or take legal action. 4. **Seek Mediation** – Many cities offer mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. 5. **File a Complaint** – If you suspect discrimination, file with the Texas Commission on Human Rights. For habitability issues, you can contact local housing authorities. ### When to Seek Legal Advice - If the landlord refuses to make necessary repairs. - If you’re being evicted without proper notice. - If you believe your rights are being violated (e.g., illegal entry, harassment). - If you’re unsure how to proceed with a repair‑and‑deduct situation. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and does not constitute legal advice. For specific legal questions or situations, consult a licensed attorney in Texas.
